::: {.session-lead}
**Can governments reduce health inequalities—and what does it take to do so?**
After examining the patterns, explanations and consequences of health
inequalities, we turn to policies that have made a difference. We compare
four historical episodes of declining health inequalities, consider the
political conditions that made reform possible, and ask whether effective
policies also enjoy public support.
:::

**Today's questions:** Which policies work? Why is reducing health inequalities difficult? How do public attitudes and politics shape policy responses?

**Learning objectives:** Compare policy approaches and historical cases; identify four mechanisms for reducing inequalities; distinguish absolute and relative gaps; and explain political barriers to effective policy.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Mandatory reading

@bambraGettingBetterPolicy2025a, *Getting Better: The Policy and
Politics of Reducing Health Inequalities* (Policy Press).

**Chapter 6**, *Waxing and waning: the four
levellers of health inequalities* (pp. 92–115). For political
implications, also see Chapter 7 (pp. 116–130). Chapters 2–5 develop the
four national case studies.

While reading, identify the **four levellers**. Which were most important
in each country, and why is it difficult to isolate the effect of any
single reform?
:::

::: {style="height: 1.5rem;"}
:::

## 1. From explaining inequalities to reducing them

We have examined the patterns and causes of health inequalities. We
now turn to **what governments can do to reduce them**.

Three policy goals are worth distinguishing:

- **Improve population health** overall.
- **Improve health among disadvantaged groups.**
- **Reduce health inequalities** between groups.

These goals are not identical. Consider a hypothetical reduction in
mortality rates (per 100,000 people):

| Socioeconomic group | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Lower socioeconomic position | 1,000 | 600 |
| Higher socioeconomic position | 500 | 250 |

Both groups benefit, but inequality changes differently depending on
how it is measured:

- **Absolute gap:** 500 → 350 (decreases).
- **Relative ratio:** 2.0 → 2.4 (increases).

Mackenbach argues that reducing **absolute inequalities** is often a
more realistic policy goal, even when relative inequalities persist
[@mackenbachHealthInequalitiesPersistence2019, ch. 6;
@mackenbachRethinkingHealthInequalities2020].

::: {.menti-prompt}
**WARM-UP**

Would you consider this policy successful? Should governments
prioritise reducing absolute or relative inequalities?
:::

### Why is reducing health inequality so difficult?

Health inequalities are often described as a **"wicked problem"**, with interacting causes and no simple solution. Key challenges include:

- **Complex causes:** Social, economic and behavioural factors interact.
- **Reverse causality:** Poor health can itself cause socioeconomic disadvantage.
- **Lifestyle drift:** Structural policy ambitions often become individual behaviour interventions.
- **Political constraints:** Evidence alone does not guarantee policy action or sustained implementation.

Reducing health inequalities therefore requires **coordinated, large-scale and politically sustained policies** [@bambraGettingBetterPolicy2025a]. Moreover, evidence about the *causes* of health inequalities does not necessarily establish which *policies* will reduce them [@mackenbachHealthInequalitiesPersistence2019, ch. 6].

### Looking upstream: The policy determinants of health

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Political choices and institutions] --> B[Social protection, economic<br/>policy and regulation]
    A --> C[Healthcare access and <br/>public services]
    B --> D[Income, housing, work and  <br/>neighbourhood conditions]
    C --> D
    D --> E[Material, psychosocial and  <br/>behavioural exposures]
    E --> F[Health outcomes and  <br/>health inequalities]
    classDef policy fill:#f2f5f9,stroke:#536579,color:#1a2530
    class A,B,C policy
```

*The political economy perspective asks not only why particular risk
factors are unequally distributed, but also which policies produce or
change that distribution* [@bambraGettingBetterPolicy2025a, ch. 1].

::: {style="height: 1.8rem;"}
:::

## 2. Four historical episodes of narrowing health inequalities

Rather than reviewing only small interventions, @bambraGettingBetterPolicy2025a
look back at periods in which **health gaps actually narrowed**. Their
four country cases differ in institutions, period and policy mix. This
makes comparison informative, but also limits simple causal attribution.

### United States: The Great Society (1960s)

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
![President Lyndon B. Johnson signing the Medicare legislation, 30 July 1965.<br> Photograph source: [White House Press Office.](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2023/05/16/president-most-blame-spiraling-national-debt-is/)](images/johnson.jpg){fig-align="center" width="85%"}
:::

- **Policy package:** anti-poverty programmes, food assistance,
  educational investment, Medicare and Medicaid, desegregation and
  civil rights legislation, and expanded political rights.
- **Observed change:** reductions in racial and income-related gaps in
  infant and premature mortality from the mid-1960s into the 1970s.
- **Why it mattered:** health-relevant living conditions and access to
  public services changed alongside the political inclusion of groups
  previously excluded or discriminated against.
- **Qualification:** the reforms occurred together, and evidence for the
  independent contribution of expanded medical insurance is more
  limited than for some other parts of the package.

### Brazil: Democratisation and social reform (1980s–2000s)

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
![Mass demonstration of the Diretas Já movement in São Paulo, 1984.<br>Photograph source: [Brazilian Federal Senate archive](https://www12.senado.leg.br/noticias/materias/2024/04/22/senado-comemora-40-anos-das-diretas-ja-nesta-sexta).](images/brazil.jpg){fig-align="center" width="85%"}
:::

- **Policy package:** a constitutional right to health and expansion of
  the public health system (*Sistema Único de Saúde*, SUS), the Family
  Health Programme, cash transfers, minimum-wage increases and new
  opportunities for political participation.
- **Observed change:** substantial reductions in infant mortality and in
  geographical and socioeconomic inequalities in childhood health.
- **Why it mattered:** healthcare improvements were combined with
  policies tackling poverty and exclusion, with larger potential gains
  for previously underserved populations.
- **Qualification:** many programmes expanded together, and the precise
  contribution of each to declining mortality is difficult to identify.

### Germany: Reunification (from 1990)

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
![Crowds gathering at the Berlin Wall by the Brandenburg Gate, November 1989.<br> Photograph source: [De Morgen.](https://www.demorgen.be/nieuws/een-journalist-van-de-morgen-was-erbij-toen-de-berlijnse-muur-viel-ze-geloofden-mij-eerst-niet-op-de-redactie~b60df89f/)](images/berlin.jpg){fig-align="center" width="85%"}
:::

- **Policy package:** the incorporation of eastern Germany into western
  social insurance, pensions, healthcare, infrastructure and other
  institutions, alongside improvements in living conditions.
- **Observed change:** the East–West **life-expectancy gap** narrowed
  sharply; the gap for women had largely disappeared by around 2010,
  while the gap for men remained smaller but persisted.
- **Why it mattered:** major institutional and material changes were
  introduced over a relatively short period.
- **Qualification:** reunification is a particularly large policy
  shock, but a bundle of changes—not a clean experiment isolating the
  effect of pensions or healthcare alone.

### England: National Health Inequalities Strategy (1997–2010)

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
![Tony Blair speaking at the London School of Economics, 12 March 2002.<br> Photograph source: [Wikimedia Commons.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Tony%20Blair%2C%202002.jpg)](images/blair.jpg){fig-align="center" width="85%"}
:::


- **Policy package:** explicit inequality targets, additional NHS and
  primary-care investment, early-years and family support, poverty
  reduction, and programmes targeted at disadvantaged areas.
- **Observed change:** some local and cause-specific inequalities
  improved during the strategy, and later analyses found more favourable
  trends in certain geographic mortality gaps. But the overall national
  targets for narrowing life-expectancy and infant-mortality gaps were
  **not achieved**.
- **Why it mattered:** health inequality reduction became a national
  political objective linked to explicit targets, funding and coordinated
  action across sectors.
- **Qualification:** @mackenbachHealthInequalitiesPersistence2019
  (ch. 6) regards the national result as largely disappointing, despite
  implementation of many planned measures. He points to weak evidence
  for some interventions, inappropriate policy entry points and
  insufficient population-wide reach. @bambraGettingBetterPolicy2025a
  emphasise the more favourable developments in particular outcomes and
  places. The distinction illustrates why **outcome, measure, period
  and comparison group** matter when evaluating success.

| Case | Main policy emphasis | Inequality dimension | Key lesson |
|---|---|---|---|
| **US, 1960s** | Poverty, civil rights, medical access | Racial and income gaps | Political inclusion and redistribution can reinforce one another. |
| **Brazil, 1980s–2000s** | Universal healthcare, transfers, democratisation | Infant mortality; regional and social gaps | Combining social and healthcare policy can yield large gains. |
| **Germany, from 1990** | Institutional integration and social protection | East–West life expectancy | Large-scale institutional change can narrow regional differences. |
| **England, 1997–2010** | Explicit targets and cross-government investment | Deprived versus other areas | Mixed evidence: some gains, but headline inequality targets missed. |

*Comparative evidence and qualifications: @bambraGettingBetterPolicy2025a,
chs. 2–6; @mackenbachHealthInequalitiesPersistence2019, ch. 6.*

::: {.menti-prompt}
**DISCUSSION | What makes these cases convincing?**

1. Which case provides the strongest evidence that *policy* reduced
   health inequalities rather than merely coinciding with a change?
2. Is a **policy package** an analytical weakness (hard to isolate
   effects), a practical strength (complementary reforms), or both?
3. Which health indicators and social or geographical groups are used
   to define success? What might these measures miss?
:::

::: {style="height: 2rem;"}
:::

## 3. The four levellers of health inequalities

Across the cases, @bambraGettingBetterPolicy2025a identify four
recurring mechanisms. They are not four mutually exclusive policies;
rather, they describe **routes through which different policy packages
can make health outcomes more equal**.

| Leveller | Typical instruments | How it may reduce health inequalities |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Welfare-state expansion** | Income support, pensions, child benefits, education and housing investment | Improves access to resources and reduces exposure to deprivation. |
| **2. Greater economic equality** | Minimum wages, labour protections, collective bargaining, redistribution | Narrows differences in earnings, security and working conditions. |
| **3. Improved healthcare access** | Universal coverage, affordable care, primary care and service investment | Reduces unequal barriers to effective prevention and treatment. |
| **4. Political incorporation** | Voting rights, representation, trade unions, participatory institutions | Gives disadvantaged groups greater voice and influence over collective decisions. |

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
### Why healthcare alone is not enough

Better medical access can reduce **treatable** health gaps. But many
inequalities arise before someone reaches the healthcare system—in
education, income, working conditions and living environments.
The historical cases suggest that **combining policies** is often more
promising than relying on a single sector
[@bambraGettingBetterPolicy2025a, ch. 6].
:::

### Are policies stronger together?

The mechanisms can **reinforce one another**. Income security may help
people benefit from healthcare, while political incorporation can make
social programmes more responsive and durable. However, the cases do
not identify a universally optimal policy mix.

### Policy success can be temporary

The four cases share another feature: **none eliminated health
inequalities, and their gains were not fully sustained**. Reforms can
be reversed, eroded by underfunding or offset by economic and political
change. This is a reason to distinguish **adoption, implementation,
effectiveness and durability** [@bambraGettingBetterPolicy2025a,
chs. 6–7].

## 4. A critical perspective: Why have health inequalities persisted?

The four historical cases show that **policy can matter**, but
@mackenbachRethinkingHealthInequalities2020 challenges some optimistic
assumptions about how readily socioeconomic health gaps can be reduced.
His argument rests on three connected points.

### 1. Causes of inequality are not identical to effective policy levers

Socioeconomic position and health are strongly associated, but the
relationship may reflect a combination of **social causation, reverse
causation and selection or confounding**. Mackenbach argues that some
causal claims, particularly about income and education, have been harder
to establish using rigorous designs than is often assumed. This does
**not** mean that material conditions are irrelevant. It means that
policies to reduce disadvantage cannot be assumed automatically to
remove every mechanism producing health inequality
[@mackenbachHealthInequalitiesPersistence2019, chs. 2, 6;
@mackenbachRethinkingHealthInequalities2020].

### 2. The welfare-state paradox

Some of Europe's most generous welfare states have **large relative
socioeconomic inequalities in mortality**. Mackenbach highlights the
role of inequalities in smoking, alcohol-related harm and other risk
factors, which redistribution alone has not eliminated. This calls for
**both structural policies and effective, equitable prevention and
healthcare**—without treating health behaviours as merely unrestricted
individual choices [@mackenbachHealthInequalitiesPersistence2019,
ch. 6; @mackenbachRethinkingHealthInequalities2020].

### 3. Interventions must reach enough people to change population outcomes

A programme can be beneficial for participants yet too small to shift
national inequality measures. The English experience illustrates the
distance between **adopting a strategy, implementing programmes,
improving individual outcomes and reducing population-level gaps**.
Mackenbach therefore recommends realistic targets, careful evaluation
and greater attention to **absolute inequality**, especially when
population health is improving [@mackenbachHealthInequalitiesPersistence2019,
ch. 6].

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### Complementary or competing lessons?

**Bambra, Lynch and Smith:** Historical episodes of narrower health gaps
show that political choices and combinations of social, healthcare and
political reforms can make a difference.

**Mackenbach:** The results of deliberate inequality-reduction policies
have often been disappointing. We should distinguish causal mechanisms,
measure outcomes carefully, and avoid promising reductions that the
available evidence and feasible scale cannot support.

These perspectives are **not mutually exclusive**: the empirical question
is *which policy, for which population, on which outcome, over what time
horizon, and relative to which counterfactual?*
:::


## 5. Learning across countries?

The historical cases provide evidence that large-scale reform **can**
reduce health inequalities. But transferring policies requires more than
copying an intervention from one country to another.

For your comparison, examine five questions:

1. **Problem and target:** Which inequality is the policy intended to
   reduce—income, education, racial or regional differences, and which
   health outcomes?
2. **Policy mechanism:** Which of the four levellers does it use? Through
   what causal pathway should it improve the distribution of health?
3. **Evidence:** Is success established by trends, before–after
   comparisons, quasi-experiments or combinations of evidence? What
   alternative explanations remain?
4. **Institutions:** Which level of government has authority and resources
   to act? How do political coalitions and administrative capacity matter?
5. **Public support and durability:** Who benefits, who bears costs,
   who opposes reform, and what would make the policy sustainable?

### Mini-workshop: Policy transfer to Switzerland

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### Group task (15–20 minutes)

**Choose one case:** US Great Society, Brazil, German reunification or
England's Health Inequalities Strategy.

Prepare a **three-minute briefing** for Swiss policymakers:

- **One intervention or policy package** worth considering;
- **One mechanism** through which it might narrow health inequalities;
- **One obstacle** arising from Swiss institutions, financing or public
  acceptance;
- **One indicator or research design** to evaluate whether it worked.

You do **not** need to claim that a historical policy can be transferred
unchanged. The aim is to identify which underlying mechanism might be
adapted—and under what conditions.
:::

### A final question about scale

Local services, including those visited at Tragwerk and LUPS Drop-in,
can address immediate needs and barriers to care. **How can such local
interventions be connected to policies that change the structural
production of disadvantage?**

::: {style="height: 1.8rem;"}
:::

## 6. Key takeaways

- **Policies can reduce health inequalities**, but attributing effects to individual interventions is difficult.
- **Four mechanisms matter:** social protection, economic equality, healthcare access and political inclusion.
- **Measurement matters:** absolute and relative inequalities can move in opposite directions.
- **Evidence matters:** identifying causes does not establish which policies will effectively reduce inequalities.
- **Politics matters:** successful policies require public support, institutional capacity and sustained implementation.

**Final discussion:** Which structural policy should Switzerland prioritise to reduce health inequalities over the next decade? How would you evaluate its success?
